method: CDM (Critical Decision Method) + ACTA (Applied Cognitive Task Analysis)

turns.speaker: Keystone
turns.text: Good morning, Hui Fen. I'm Keystone, the AI interviewer for the Expert Onboarding Call. Today we'll capture your judgement on tenant communications during water-leak and related incidents. Ready?

turns.speaker: Lim Hui Fen
turns.text: Ready. Nine years in property and tenant-experience management across the Keppel REIT portfolio — offices, a data centre, logistics, residences. Comms during an incident is where we either keep tenants calm or make a bad day worse, so I'm happy to walk through it.

turns.speaker: Keystone
turns.text: Walk me through a recent incident where the comms really mattered — or where a wrong message would have caused a problem.

turns.speaker: Lim Hui Fen
turns.text: The Harbourfront One L28 leak last year is the one. A bank tenant on L27 had water dripping through their ceiling. The technical team was isolating, but my job was the tenant — what they knew, when, and who approved it. The temptation is to over-promise or under-inform, and both are mistakes. So we have a fixed comms discipline.

turns.speaker: Keystone
turns.text: Let's put the comms in order. What goes out first, how many minutes in, to whom, and who signs it off?

turns.speaker: Lim Hui Fen
turns.text: First notice goes out within thirty minutes, full stop — and only to the tenants actually affected, not the whole building. It says what happened, where, what we're doing about it, when the next update is, and a contact number. No cause, no liability, no promise of a fix time. And it does not go out without a named human approving it — me or my delegate. I'm not having an automated message sent to a tenant on its own.

turns.speaker: Keystone
turns.text: What would someone new to tenant comms most likely get wrong when the tenant asks when it'll be fixed?

turns.speaker: Lim Hui Fen
turns.text: Tenants always ask 'when will it be fixed?'. You cannot answer that until the source is confirmed and isolation is done. I've seen a colleague promise two hours and it took six because the riser joint was worse than expected. So you say: our team is on site working to isolate the source, and we will provide an update on the repair timeline at the next update. You give them the next update time, not a completion time.

turns.speaker: Keystone
turns.text: Is there anything you would never put in a message, no matter how much pressure you're under — the cause, for example?

turns.speaker: Lim Hui Fen
turns.text: Do not tell the tenant what caused it until someone has actually confirmed it. Not 'appears to be', not 'we believe'. If the technician hasn't laid eyes on it and told you, you say the investigation is ongoing. The moment you say 'a pipe burst' and it turns out to be the sprinkler line, you've handed the tenant ammunition for a claim. Wait for Technical Services or the LEW to confirm.

turns.speaker: Keystone
turns.text: Big picture — which tenants need to hear from you, and from whom? Is a bank anchor tenant different?

turns.speaker: Lim Hui Fen
turns.text: A bank anchor tenant — or any tenant with a notification SLA in their lease — gets a phone call from the account manager within thirty minutes. Not the technician, not the Duty Manager, and not just an email. The account manager picks up the phone, then the written notice follows. The bank's facilities director needs to hear a human voice, not a template, when their trading floor is at risk.

turns.speaker: Keystone
turns.text: What must never go into a message, whoever approves it — personal data, for example?

turns.speaker: Lim Hui Fen
turns.text: PII, PDPA — you cannot put Tenant B's name in Tenant A's notice, and you cannot CC multiple tenants on one email. Each tenant gets their own notice. Unit numbers, individual names, contact details are masked in anything visible to a lower role. Lease terms and rental rates never go in any message. I had a junior put three tenants on one chain and we got a PDPA complaint — never again.

turns.speaker: Keystone
turns.text: Compare an office tenant, the bank, and a data-centre client. How is one different from the other two?

turns.speaker: Lim Hui Fen
turns.text: Data-centre clients are different. They don't get tenant-experience messages. The critical facilities manager handles the SLA notification — event reference, impact assessment, resolution window if you have one. The CFM approves it, not me. Different template, different channel, different approver. If you send a standard tenant notice to a hyperscale client, their legal team is on the phone before you've finished typing.

turns.speaker: Keystone
turns.text: Suppose the FSM orders an evacuation while your first notice is still waiting for approval. Does the evacuation message wait for you?

turns.speaker: Lim Hui Fen
turns.text: No — never. If the FSM or the FCC calls an evacuation or a stay-put, that goes out immediately over the PA and mass notification. It doesn't wait for me — the FSM has the authority, not Tenant Experience. What I do is log it and follow up with a written notice, and that written notice still goes through approval like any other. The approval rule is for our messages, not for life safety.

extracted_rules_summary.TE-01: First notice to affected tenants within 30 min; named human approval before send
extracted_rules_summary.TE-02: No completion-time promise before source confirmed and isolation complete
extracted_rules_summary.TE-03: No unverified cause claims in outbound messages
extracted_rules_summary.TE-04: Bank anchor tenant gets account-manager phone call within 30 min
extracted_rules_summary.TE-05: PII masking on all outbound messages (PDPA)
extracted_rules_summary.TE-06: DC clients get SLA notice via critical facilities manager, not TE comms
extracted_rules_summary.TE-07: Life-safety instruction from FSM/FCC goes out immediately without comms approval; written follow-up still approved
